paper_title: Information Games: Strategic Crowding and Firm Repositioning in Language-Model Space

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: When firms respond to new market opportunities, their capacity choices alter the future discounted free cash flows available to both competitors and investors. In competitive markets, these investment decisions publicized in news articles and analyst reports, measuring the changes in capital structure, product mix, firm leadership, risk exposure and operating procedure made by the firm. Modern search engines rely on Large Language Models to measure the relevancy of source documents to given search query. These measurements let researchers represent these news articles as clouds of dense vectors whose information geometry reflects the dissimilarity of firms over time. Building on Xu et al. (2022), we develop a model of costly competitive adjustment in which firms allocate capacity in which firms make firm capacity adjustment towards free cash flow shocks. Using a novel sandwich estimator, we analyse the sign and magnitude of this predicted adjustment using multi-agent simulation, and validate our findings on a sample of news and analyst reports from Nasdaq-listed companies between 2018-2022.

sections.title: Start
sections.content: Information Games: Strategic Crowding and Firm Repositioning in Language-Model Space Marcus Gawronsky, Chun-Sung Huang Department of Finance and Tax, University of Cape Town October 2026 Abstract Firms reallocate capacity as market opportunities change, altering competitors profitability and the cash flows investors anticipate. We extend the multi-contest framework of Xu et al. (2022) to explain how competition and adjustment costs shape firms changing positions and their exposure to free cash flow disturbances. The model establishes equilibrium properties and comparative statics, linking gradual operating adjustment to financial responses when new economic opportunities arrive. In restricted two-opportunity economy, firms with greater initial exposure experience larger return responses to positive exogenous free cash flow shocks. As other firms expand toward that opportunity, their news distributions approach the initial distributions of those competitors. Under common reporting intensity and the stated timing conditions, this mechanism implies nonnegative expected local association between financial returns and movement toward competitors in information space. We develop novel sandwich estimator that relates changes in Wasserstein distances between corporate-news distributions to excess returns weighted by article timing. Multi-agent simulations show how limited coverage obscures small operating adjustments and how changing coverage can generate similar observed movements. In an application using Nasdaq-listed firms our empirical study finds small positive association across alternative specifications. Together, these results give an economic foundation for studying firms changing economic footprints through financial news and clarifies how competition and information production shape firms investment decisions. Keywords: Competitive adjustment; Rival feedback; Operating exposure; Distributional measurement JEL classification: D43; G14; L25; C

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: A manufacturer responding to stronger demand for industrial automation must decide how much capacity to add and which activities to expand. Its investment changes the margins available to competing manufacturers, whose responses in turn affect the attractiveness of that expansion. Adjusting capacity takes time, while news of its cash-flow consequences can change firms valuations before the operating response is complete. These linked decisions change firms positions relative to their competitors and create connection between investment, financial valuation, and the information reported about firms. Firms engage in several activities at once, and their competitive positions depend on the composition of those activities as well as their scale. This allocation of capacity defines 1 firms economic footprint. Recent work by Gawronsky and Huang (2026) represents firms through distributions of financial-news embeddings, preserving differences among the articles associated with each firm rather than reducing its coverage to single average. Such distributions provide way to compare firms positions in information space. Understanding how firms economic footprints evolve requires an account of the choices that change their activities. Spatial and multi-market competition provide foundation for that account. Since Hotelling (1929), models of product positioning have linked firms locations to the demand they serve. Research on strategic substitutes and complements and on networked competition shows how firms choices affect rivals across markets (Bulow et al., 1985; Bimpikis et al., 2019). The multi-contest framework of Xu et al. (2022) formalizes such interdependence when players allocate resources across overlapping contests. We adapt that framework to firms allocating operating capacity across activities that serve related customer demands, where each firms expansion changes the contribution margins available to its competitors. Firms differ in the activities they can pursue at low cost, while increasing capacity brings additional expense. We establish conditions for unique Nash equilibrium and derive how opportunity and cost changes affect capacity allocations, business mix, and rivals responses. To study repositioning over time, we introduce costs of changing inherited capacity. Each periods operating choices form Nash equilibrium conditional on the previous allocation, so adjustment unfolds gradually as competitors respond to one another. Investors value the cash flows generated along this path at constant discount factor. They incorporate anticipated changes in cash flows into firms valuations immediately, even as operating capacity adjusts over subsequent periods. In restricted two-opportunity economy, firms with greater initial exposure experience larger return responses to positive exogenous free cash flow shocks. The shock improves one opportunity relative to the other, inducing firms to reallocate capacity toward it. If news coverage reflects the relative allocation of operating capacity, firm increasing its exposure becomes closer to the initial news distributions of more-exposed competitors and farther from those of less-exposed competitors. With fixed reference distributions and the stated conditions on news timing and observation errors, these responses imply nonnegative expected local association between relative financial returns and decreases in the target firms distance to other firms. This result gives competitive repositioning an observable implication in information space. Financial news is itself produced through economic choices. Investors seek information about material changes in investment, products, and cash-flow prospects, while publishers and corporate disclosures influence which developments receive coverage (Gentzkow and Shapiro, 2006). Following research that uses corporate text to study product-market relationships (Hoberg and Phillips, 2016), we represent firms articles as mixture of distributions associated with its activities. The relative weight of each activity depends on both operating capacity and the intensity of coverage. When coverage per unit of capacity is equal across activities, news composition follows the firms business mix. Changes in coverage can also alter the reported distribution while capacity remains unchanged. We measure differences between firms article distributions using squared Wasserstein distance. Optimal transport finds minimum-cost matching between the distributions of article embeddings, capturing changes in their composition even when their average vectors change little. For each firm, we measure whether its annual news distribution moves closer to or farther from other firms distributions fixed at their 2018 positions. We compare these changes with the reference firms daily excess returns, summed with weights determined by the proportion of the target firms articles published after each return date. Centering 2 both measures across reference firms within target-year produces an estimator of the predicted relative association. Multi-agent simulations assess this estimator using operating paths and return responses generated by the model. Under equal reporting intensity, the population coefficient is positive in each of sixteen simulated news histories, yet only 53.1% of article samples at observed coverage yield numerically resolved positive estimate. Increasing article coverage improves recovery, although measurement error remains substantial. In separate observation counterfactual, changing the relative coverage of activities also produces positive alignment while operating capacities are held fixed. These experiments show how article sampling and the production of news affect the ability to observe competitive adjustment. We apply the estimator to financial news and returns for 100 Nasdaq-listed firms from 2018 to 2022. Across four specifications, firms movements relative to fixed reference distributions are positively associated with those reference firms relative weighted excess returns, although the relationship is small. The evidence is descriptive, while the simulations establish why changes in news cannot be interpreted as changes in operating capacity alone. Together, the theory and empirical analysis extend the study of distribution-valued firms from comparisons of their reported economic footprints to an economic account of why those footprints may change over time. The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 reviews the related literature. Section 3 develops the economic model, its directional prediction, the estimator and the restricted-form hypothesis. Section 4 evaluates the estimator and its measurement uncertainty through multi-agent simulations, then describes the corporate data and empirical design. Section 5 presents the results and their economic interpretation. Section 6 concludes.

sections.title: 2 Literature Review
sections.content: Spatial competition provides foundation for understanding how firms positions influence demand and the profitability of their decisions. In Hotelling (1929), consumers choose between firms by weighing prices against transportation costs, making location an important determinant of competitive advantage. firms decision to reposition consequently depends on the customers it can attract and the responses of its competitors. These interactions become more complex when firms operate across several markets. Bulow et al. (1985) establish how strategic substitutes and complements connect competitive decisions, while Bimpikis et al. (2019) examine how competition and production linkages transmit shocks through networked markets. Together, these contributions motivate studying firm positioning through the allocation of resources across related activities and the competitive responses those allocations generate. The multi-contest framework of Xu et al. (2022) provides the closest theoretical founIn their model, players allocate costly effort across contests, dation for our analysis. receiving shares of prizes that depend on their allocations relative to those of competitors. Their equilibrium characterization and comparative statics establish how competitive interactions transmit changes in incentives through network of contests. We adapt this proportional-share structure to firms allocating operating capacity across activities that serve overlapping customer demands. Capacity determines firms ability to serve each demand opportunity, while rivals compete for the same available contribution margins. The resulting allocation problem admits discrete-choice interpretation when capacity represents varieties or outlets (McFadden, 1974; Train, 2009). Building on the equilibrium and sensitivity methods of Xu et al. (2022), we establish uniqueness and characterize firms 3 responses to changes in market opportunities and costs under the conditions of our capacity model. Competitive repositioning also depends on the costs of changing existing investments. Sweeting (2013) studies forward-looking product positioning in differentiated markets, demonstrating the importance of adjustment costs for firms decisions. We introduce persistence through quadratic costs of changing inherited capacity, with firms making sequential Nash choices as market opportunities and competitors allocations evolve. The resulting operating path determines the cash flows investors anticipate following an exogenous free cash flow shock. Berk et al. (1999) relate investment opportunities to security returns through changes in assets and growth options. We follow this connection between operating opportunities and financial valuation, discounting the cash flows generated along the adjustment path. Firm valuations can consequently respond when new information arrives, while firms operating allocations adjust over time. Corporate disclosures and financial news provide information about firms activities and their competitive environments. Hoberg and Phillips (2016) demonstrate how corporate text can reveal product-market relationships and differences in competitive positioning, while Gentzkow et al. (2019) establish methodological foundations for using text as economic data. The information available to investors also reflects the incentives governing its production. Gentzkow and Shapiro (2006) study how reputation and reporting incentives influence news content, providing an economic motivation for considering differences in the coverage of firms activities. We incorporate these considerations through an observation model in which firms news distribution depends on both its operating capacity and the relative intensity of reporting across activities. Representing corporate information as distribution preserves variation among the activities and perspectives reflected in individual articles. Kusner et al. (2015) develop transport-based comparisons of word embeddings, while Gawronsky and Huang (2026) use Wasserstein geometry to study covariance envelopes from language-model representations. Optimal transport compares distributions through the minimum cost of matching their probability mass, retaining information about their composition and dispersion that may be lost when articles are represented by single average vector. This provides natural basis for comparing firms positions in information space and measuring changes in those positions over time. We extend this literature by deriving an economic mechanism for changes in firms economic footprints. Costly capacity adjustment and competitive responses determine how firms react to changing opportunities, while financial valuation reflects the cash-flow consequences of those decisions. In restricted two-opportunity economy, initial exposure determines the ordering of firms return responses and, under the specified reporting conditions, the direction of movement toward other firms initial news distributions. The resulting nonnegative expected local association provides the theoretical basis for the estimator developed in the following section.

sections.content: To assess how reliably finite samples of financial news recover the positive association predicted by the model, we develop multi-agent simulation of the economy in Section 3, whose population coefficients are known. sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Design
sections.content: The experiment follows competitive adjustment after small exogenous free cash flow shocks, keeping operating movements close to the local setting of the directional prediction. Sampling articles along these paths reveals how well the estimator detects small reallocations at the coverage observed in the corporate data. The competitive economy has 100 firms with canonical interior baseline shares pi = i/101, total capacity one, two activities and two opportunities. Outside appeal and baseline opportunity levels equal one, with cost curvature ν = 1/(4D2), where = 51, linear costs supporting the interior origin, and adjustment weight κ = = ν + 1/D2. The 60 monthly ticks begin from stationary conditions, which we label 2018 for comparison with the corporate sample, followed by independent permanent innovations of 0.001 at ticks 18, 30, 42 and 54 that raise one opportunity and lower the other. We evaluate all sixteen sign histories and assign each equal weight. At monthly discounting δ = 0.951/12, we compute return responses using the infinite permanent-response resolvent in (7), while the operating engine solves every contemporaneous joint Nash stage at the actual positive opportunity levels. In the first responding month after the first innovation, absolute changes in normalized operating shares range from 0.0316 to 0.0502 percentage points across firms and histories, with the largest absolute departure from an origin share over the complete paths reaching 0.203 percentage points. These small movements specify the local signal tested in this economy. The baseline article budget uses the firm-year article counts and frozen empirical monthly date distributions of the primary corporate sample described in Section 4.4. The next budgets multiply every count by four and sixteen. For each history, 160 independent article panels use nested count increments across budgets and shared sampled monthly counts across reporting regimes. The same dated counts determine annual article laws and article-timing weights, and each sampled origin law is reused wherever it serves as reference. Because multinomial month and atom counts can leave unequal masses on antipodal atoms, we compute transport exactly on the axis support, which retains that asymmetry. Reusing each solved operating path across redraws isolates article measurement variation around the same economic response. The control holds reporting laws fixed rather than solving new competitive equilibrium.

sections.title: 4.3 Measurement Uncertainty and Inference
sections.content: The spread of finite-article estimates provides benchmark for assessing whether redrawing articles from an observed archive represents that measurement uncertainty. We generate independent archives from the common-reporting, stationary and reporting-only laws, retaining 100 firms and observed article coverage, then apply the corporate article-redraw procedure within each archive. Across 160 archives per history, each with 199 inner redraws, the broad redraw ranges give near-nominal containment of the population coefficients. Containment and detection answer different questions. Under the positive-target commonreporting and reporting-only laws, the fifth percentile exceeds zero in 4.8% and 5.9% of attempts, respectively. Thus, intervals that broadly capture measurement uncertainty rarely distinguish these small positive population coefficients from zero. Under stationary reporting, the target is zero, so the corresponding 4.4% is instead null-control rejection frequency. Uncertainty across independently sampled firms concerns different target from article selection around fixed operating paths. For each target coefficient, we generate 2500 independent panels, each consisting of iid firm histories. Increasing the number of firms from 16 to 100 raises coverage of the candidate one-sided 95% lower bound from 89.5% to 93.8%. Zero-null rejection falls from 10.5% to 6.2% (Monte Carlo SE 0.48 percentage points at 100 firms). These generated-history panels preserve dependence across years and comparison roles under the specified iid sampling law, although they are not jointly solved competitive economies. Appendix gives the sampling designs, target containment and Monte Carlo errors.

sections.title: 4.4 Empirical Design and Data
sections.content: To examine whether the association that the simulation recovers only imperfectly also appears in corporate news, we apply the estimator of Section 3.5 to 100 Nasdaq-listed firms over five article years from 2018 through 2022, giving four transitions ending in 20192022. We measure semantic similarity between articles by embedding them with Qwen3Embedding-4B (Zhang et al., 2025), four-billion-parameter transformer developed for information retrieval. Because the model postdates the sample, these vectors give retrospective representation of the articles. We assess the role of representation by comparing its native 2560-dimensional vectors with compressed 64-dimensional representation. As the 12 model is trained with Matryoshka representation learning (Kusupati et al., 2022), we obtain the compressed vectors from the first 64 coordinates of each native vector, renormalized to unit length. We also compare two article samples within each representation to measure sensitivity to the amount and balance of coverage. While the expanded sample contains 43 720 existing article embeddings, the matched sample restricts these to the first 128 per firm in URL-hash order after the corpus date and body-length filters, giving 12 800 articles. Taking the native expanded specification as primary, we treat the other three as diagnostic comparisons, none selected by its financial coefficient. All retain the same roster, origin references and annual financial windows, but changing the article sample changes both geometry and the dates entering (11). For 199 paired conditional article redraws, each firm-year cloud is redrawn once within its canonical and additional-article strata and reused in every target and reference role. Origin draws remain shared across all transitions and representations, and the return weights are recomputed from the sampled article dates. The reported 2.5th, 5th and 97.5th percentiles describe article-selection sensitivity conditional on the observed articles, firms, financial histories and four annual environments. Shared stories, common shocks and reused references make the 39 600 directional coordinates dependent.

sections.title: 5.2 Discussion
sections.content: The findings provide an economic interpretation of how firms economic footprints can evolve in response to changing market opportunities. Distribution-valued representations allow researchers to compare firms through the information associated with their activities, but changes in those distributions do not, by themselves, explain the economic decisions underlying repositioning. Our model connects these movements to strategic competition. When firms adjust capacity across overlapping activities, their decisions affect competitors margins, while adjustment costs make the response to new opportunities gradual. In the restricted two-opportunity economy, initial operating exposures determine both the ordering of return responses and the direction of movement relative to competitors initial news distributions. This establishes mechanism through which competitive adjustment can generate systematic changes in firms reported economic footprints, extending distributionbased comparisons beyond static measures of similarity. The distinction between financial valuation and operating adjustment is central to this mechanism. Investors can capitalize the anticipated cash-flow consequences of an exogenous free cash flow shock when information arrives, whereas firms adjust their operating allocations over subsequent periods. Return responses and changes in reported economic footprints consequently need not coincide in time. The article-timing weights in our estimator connect reference firms daily excess returns to the subsequent appearance of information about the adjusting firm. This construction captures directional relationship between weighted excess returns and changes in the firms reported economic footprint, rather than identifying structural adjustment speed. Its economic interpretation depends jointly on initial exposures, competitive interactions, adjustment costs, and the timing of information. The historical results reveal positive but economically small association. The estimated direction is consistent across four measurement specifications, and the primary normalized 14 association is 0.0363, corresponding to approximately 0.13% descriptive within-sample fit. Thus, the predicted ordering appears in the data but accounts for only limited component of observed information movements. This modest magnitude is compatible with gradual operating adjustment, heterogeneous responses to economic opportunities, and imperfect measurement of firms activities. The simulations clarify the last possibility: at the benchmarks small adjustment scale, finite article samples frequently fail to resolve positive population relationship, even when coverage increases substantially. They do not, however, establish which mechanism explains the small historical association. The evidence supports directional correspondence without demonstrating that the underlying operating response is either strong or uniform across firms. The reconstruction results sharpen this interpretation. In the primary specification, the restricted movement profile improves held-out reconstruction of annual news changes by only 1.47% relative to zero-change benchmark, while two alternative specifications perform worse than that benchmark. positive directional association can therefore coexist with weak reconstruction of the broader evolution of firms reported economic footprints. These findings answer different questions. The directional estimate measures whether relative movements toward reference firms correspond to their relative weighted excess returns, whereas the reconstruction exercise evaluates how well the models restricted geometric pattern describes observed changes in news distributions. The theory predicts the former under specified conditions, not complete account of the latter. Nevertheless, the weak reconstruction indicates that the historical movements contain substantial variation beyond the local theoretical approximation. The empirical evidence is consequently more informative about relative directional ordering than about the full geometry or magnitude of firms repositioning. An additional implication concerns the production of financial information itself. Corporate news reflects both underlying economic activity and the attention directed toward different activities. Under the observation model, changes in reporting intensity alter firms information distribution even when its operating allocation remains unchanged. The reporting-only simulation demonstrates that this channel can generate positive directional alignment at fixed capacities. Operating adjustment and reporting responses can therefore produce similar observed movements, potentially reinforcing or offsetting one another. This distinction is not simply source of statistical noise: it affects the economic meaning of the distances used to represent firms. The historical estimator measures changes in reported economic footprints associated with relative weighted excess returns, but does not separately identify the contributions of operating decisions and reporting intensity. Interpreting information-space movements as changes in economic activity requires assumptions about how that activity becomes observable. The stability of the estimated sign provides useful evidence about the historical association, although it does not establish its generality. The primary coefficient remains positive across annual transitions and the reported deletion exercises. At the same time, the 2020 transition contributes 41.4% of the pooled centered financial second moment, and the largest reference-firm contribution accounts for 15.1%. The financial variation informing the estimate is therefore unevenly distributed across the sample. Moreover, the theoretical prediction arises under restricted opportunity and observation conditions that need not characterize the wider corporate environment. Stability of the estimated direction should accordingly be distinguished from evidence that the same economic mechanism operates with comparable strength across firms, activities, and market conditions. Taken together, these results extend the economic interpretation of distribution-valued firms by linking changes in reported economic footprints to competitive adjustment and 15 financial valuation. Building on the multi-contest allocation framework of Xu et al. (2022), the analysis establishes how inherited capacities, strategic responses, and anticipated cash flows can jointly produce testable directional relationship in information space. The historical application identifies corresponding association, while the simulations and reconstruction exercises establish important boundaries on its interpretation. More direct tests would combine dated information about investment, production, or operating capacity with financial returns and corporate news, allowing changes in economic activity to be distinguished from changes in reporting. Such evidence could also examine whether the predicted ordering extends beyond the restricted setting considered here. The broader contribution is an economic foundation for studying firms changing economic footprints through financial news.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: Firms reallocate capacity as market opportunities change, and their decisions alter the margins available to competitors. Adjustment costs make these responses gradual, while investors can value the anticipated cash-flow consequences when news arrives. Building on Xu et al. (2022), we characterize sequential Nash capacity choices, establish equilibrium and comparative-static results, and connect firms operating paths to financial valuation. In restricted two-opportunity economy, firms with greater initial exposure experience larger return responses to positive exogenous free cash flow shocks. As another firm increases its exposure to the improving activity, its news distribution moves closer to the initial distributions of more-exposed competitors when reporting intensity is equal across activities. Under the stated conditions, this generates nonnegative expected local association between relative financial returns and changes in firms positions in information space. We investigate this prediction using squared Wasserstein distances between distributions of corporate-news embeddings and excess returns weighted by article timing. Monte Carlo experiments show that limited article coverage makes the positive population relationship difficult to recover at the small operating-adjustment scale considered. Changes in the relative coverage of activities can also produce positive association while capacities remain fixed. In sample of 100 Nasdaq-listed firms over 20182022, the estimated association is positive across four specifications but small. separate held-out exercise finds that the restricted movement pattern accounts for little of the variation in annual news distributions. By treating firms economic footprints as outcomes of strategic choices, the paper adds an explanation for how those footprints evolve to research on distribution-valued firms. The analysis also establishes why the production of financial news matters for measuring those changes: operating reallocations and shifts in coverage can have similar effects on observed distributions. Independent, dated measures of operating activity would allow future research to distinguish these mechanisms and assess the model more directly. This provides basis for studying changes in firms economic footprints through their reported activities and financial returns.
